items.body: Front Line Assembly’s “Epitaph” turns 25 this year. Metropolis Records released the electro-industrial and EBM album on 8 October 2001, the eleventh full-length studio album by the Vancouver band led by Bill Leeb and Chris Peterson. The record marked Front Line Assembly‘s return to Metropolis Records after the band left the label in October 1999. “Epitaph” runs ten tracks and 54:57, recorded at Cryogenic Studio and produced by Leeb and Peterson. Greg Reely handled mixing and engineering, Brian Gardner mastered the album, and Dave McKean supplied the artwork and design. The tracklist runs “Haloed”, “Dead Planet”, “Backlash”, “Epitaph”, “Everything Must Perish”, “Conscience”, “Decoy”, “Insolence”, “Krank It Up” and “Existance”, the last of which folds in the hidden track “Submerged” after a minute of silence. Metropolis also issued a digipak edition limited to 25,000 copies carrying that bonus track. “Everything Must Perish”, released 11 September 2001, was the only single taken from the album. Bill Leeb told Side-Line at the time that “Epitaph” broke with the band’s earlier reliance on film dialogue samples: “This is the first time we quit using movie samples.” He added: “Sampling is an artform which was criticised in the beginning, but now it’s a respected artform with big money in it. It’s a big business where I don’t feel at ease any longer.” Artoffact Records re-released ‘Epitaph’ on limited edition vinyl in 2015. About Front Line Assembly Bill Leeb founded Front Line Assembly in Vancouver, British Columbia, in 1986 after leaving Skinny Puppy, where he had performed under the stage name Wilhelm Schroeder. Rhys Fulber worked with Leeb from the same period as an early, unofficial collaborator, and Michael Balch became an official member on keyboards and programming in 1988. The band’s debut album, “The Initial Command”, came out on the Belgian label KK at the end of 1987, followed by “State of Mind” on the German label Dossier in January 1988 and “Corrosion” the same year, licensed to Wax Trax! for North America. Balch left after the Gashed Senses & Crossfire tour in 1989 to join Ministry and Revolting Cocks, and Fulber stepped in as an official member. “Gashed Senses & Crossfire” (1989) gave the band its first chart entry, with “Digital Tension Dementia” reaching No. 45 on Billboard’s Hot Dance Club Songs. “Caustic Grip” followed in 1990, the album that began Front Line Assembly’s long-running partnership with mixer and engineer Greg Reely and introduced more guitar-driven material. Chris Peterson debuted as a live percussionist on the accompanying tour before later becoming a full-time member. “Tactical Neural Implant” (1992) brought a more melodic, sample-heavy direction, and “Millennium” (1994) became the band’s first industrial metal record, featuring session guitar from Devin Townsend, who also played on “Hard Wired” (1995). Fulber left in 1997 to concentrate on producing Fear Factory, and Peterson took over his role as the band moved toward the electronica and big-beat leanings of “[FLA]vour of the Weak” (1997) and “Implode” (1999). In October 1999 the band left Metropolis Records; “Epitaph”, produced by Leeb and Peterson and issued on 8 October 2001, marked its return to that label. Peterson departed after finishing work on the album, and Fulber rejoined in 2003 for “Civilization” (2004). Beyond the main discography, Leeb has led the side project Delerium since 1987, and members have worked on Noise Unit, Conjure One (Fulber), Cyberaktif (Leeb with Skinny Puppy’s cEvin Key and Dwayne Goettel) and other spin-offs. Front Line Assembly went on to release “Artificial Soldier” (2006), “Improvised Electronic Device” (2010), “Echogenetic” (2013), “Wake Up the Coma” (2019) and “Mechanical Soul” (2021), the last featuring guest appearances from Jean-Luc De Meyer of Front 242 and Dino Cazares of Fear Factory. The band caught up with Side-Line on the state of the group in 2024, with Leeb and Fulber both still in the current lineup. “Epitaph” remains the band’s eleventh studio album and, twenty-five years on, the record that reopened its relationship with Metropolis Records.

The project’s prior full-length, “Impendum,” came out in 2004. State Of The Union signed to Infacted Recordings and released the digital EP “Mindless” in November 2018, followed by the CD album “Indupop” and the digital EP “Industrial Slither / Remixes” in early 2019, and the EP “Bad Flower” in 2020, all on Infacted Recordings. With “When Daylight Dies,” State Of The Union returns for the first time since that pair of 2023 singles, and Johann Sebastian has signaled more music to come.

items.body: Berkeley, California spoken word industrial artist Ms Xxan released the two-track single shaper of decrepitude. on October 5, 2026, through her own Bandcamp page. The single pairs its title track with “ghosted.” and follows her spoken word dark ambient album “Make Yourself the Lie” by less than a month. Ms Xxan wrote, performed, composed and produced both tracks herself. The release pairs spoken-word vocals with doom-paced, noise-industrial production in the death-industrial and harsh-noise register that runs through her catalogue. She flags the single with a content warning for lyrics that may affect mental health sensitivities. shaper of decrepitude. by Ms Xxan “shaper of decrepitude.” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp. About Ms Xxan Ms Xxan writes, performs and produces spoken word and industrial noise music from Berkeley, California. She released the nine-track spoken word dark ambient album “Make Yourself the Lie” on September 8, 2026, as a free, name-your-price download via VūMantra Records, the Berlin label founded in 2019 by Vince Gagliardi, who also records as The Nent and LAGÁN. That album carried a content warning for explicit lyrics addressing depression, and the same material also circulates as a podcast on Apple Podcasts and Audiomack. Ms Xxan handles writing, performance, composition and production on her own across both releases. With “shaper of decrepitude.”, she returned to self-releasing directly on Bandcamp, pairing the title track with “ghosted.” as a quick follow-up to the VūMantra album.

items.body: This third album from the mysterious Swiss duo Blackbook was released just before the summer and brings us a total of 12 new tracks. I have always been somewhat intrigued by this act. While their music sounds superb, it is invariably driven by massive clichés and often seems almost literally ‘lifted’ from existing songs. With “Different”, they remain true to their 80s Electro-Wave/Pop influences, yet the tracks sound somewhat more personal this time around. It may be a cliché, but the way they develop their sound—consistently delivering strong choruses—is remarkable. Every single track sounds danceable and powerful, possessing the essential catchiness this genre demands. The songs also appear to have been deliberately kept short—not a single one reaches the four-minute mark. Blackbook remains a true mystery, yet one that consistently returns with great music—clichéd or not! (Rating:8½). Listen to “Nobody Loves You”: Nobody Loves You by Blackbook About Blackbook Blackbook is a Swiss duo who perform under masks and withhold their surnames, going only by their first names, Matthias and Albert. Both had previously played in other Swiss and German acts before forming Blackbook, citing 80s and 90s music as a shared influence. The duo discussed their approach and anonymity in a Side-Line interview in 2023. The project released a series of singles before compiling them into its official debut album, “Confessions Of The Innocent” (2023), followed by “Radio Strange” (2024) and, issued just before the summer of 2026, the duo’s third album “Different”, all released through darkTunes Music Group.

items.body: Simple Minds released their twelfth studio album, “Neon Lights”, on 8 October 2001 through Eagle Records. The Scottish post-punk and new wave band’s collection of cover versions turns 25 this year, arriving as the group’s first release after a period away from active recording. “Neon Lights” was conceived as a warm-up ahead of the following year’s “Cry” and gathers Simple Minds’ versions of songs by artists including Them, David Bowie, Pete Shelley, the Patti Smith Group, Kraftwerk, the Doors, Echo and the Bunnymen, Neil Young, Roxy Music and the Velvet Underground. Frontman Jim Kerr set out the thinking behind the project at the time of release: “Neon Lights is the first time Simple Minds have put together a collection of non-original material. We thought it was appropriate at a period of looking back that we go to the very foundations of Simple Minds, which of course is the music and the bands who influenced us.” The album followed a difficult stretch for the band. Their prior record, “Our Secrets Are the Same”, had been delivered to Chrysalis but was caught up in the label’s merger with EMI, remained unreleased, and was then leaked on the internet in 2000. Discouraged by the lost momentum, band members Eddie Duffy, Mark Taylor and Mark Kerr moved on to other projects, and Jim Kerr relocated to Sicily to work part-time as a hotelier. In 2001, Kerr and guitarist Charlie Burchill began working with multi-instrumentalist Gordon “Gordy” Goudie, a former member of the Primevals, on new material intended for “Cry”. Recorded in parallel with those sessions in Glasgow, Dublin and Taormina, Sicily, “Neon Lights” was completed and released first. Simple Minds’ ‘Neon Lights’ tracklist and credits The UK edition ran ten tracks: “Gloria” (Them), “The Man Who Sold the World” (David Bowie), “Homosapien” (Pete Shelley), “Dancing Barefoot” (Patti Smith Group), “Neon Lights” (Kraftwerk), “Hello, I Love You” (the Doors), “Bring on the Dancing Horses” (Echo and the Bunnymen), “The Needle and the Damage Done” (Neil Young), “For Your Pleasure” (Roxy Music) and “All Tomorrow’s Parties” (the Velvet Underground). A US release added two further covers, “Being Boiled” (the Human League) and “Love Will Tear Us Apart” (Joy Division). The album was produced by Jim Kerr and Charlie Burchill with Gordy Goudie, except for “Gloria”, which was produced by Phunk Investigation, Daniele Tignino and Emiliano Patrik Legato; Simon Heyworth handled mastering. Two singles followed the album: the “Dancing Barefoot” EP and a series of “Homosapien” remixes. The full album is available via Spotify. About Simple Minds Simple Minds trace back to Johnny and the Self-Abusers, a Glasgow punk band formed in early 1977 by Jim Kerr, Charlie Burchill, Tony Donald and Brian McGee. That group released a single, “Saints and Sinners”, on Chiswick Records in November 1977 and split the same day. The remaining members regrouped under the name Simple Minds, drawn from a lyric in David Bowie’s “The Jean Genie”, and played their first show on 17 January 1978 in Glasgow. Duncan Barnwell joined on second guitar that January, Mick MacNeil added keyboards in March, and Derek Forbes replaced Donald on bass in April; Barnwell left by November, leaving a settled quintet of Kerr, Burchill, MacNeil, Forbes and McGee. Manager Bruce Findlay signed the band to Zoom Records, licensed to Arista, for a 1979 debut, “Life in a Day”, which reached number 30 on the UK Albums Chart. Further albums followed in quick succession: “Real to Real Cacophony” (1979), “Empires and Dance” (1980) and the double release “Sons and Fascination” / “Sister Feelings Call” (1981). Brian McGee left after those sessions and was eventually replaced by Mel Gaynor, recruited by producer Peter Walsh in 1982 and later the band’s longest-standing drummer. Released from Arista in early 1981, Simple Minds signed to Virgin Records, and “New Gold Dream” (1982) gave the band its first Billboard 200 entry and a number 3 UK placing. “Sparkle in the Rain” (1984) debuted at number 1 in the UK and was later certified Platinum, and “Once Upon a Time” (1985) reached number 1 in the UK and the Netherlands and was certified triple Platinum in Britain, driven by the US number 1 single “Don’t You (Forget About Me)” from the film “The Breakfast Club”. Bassist Derek Forbes was dismissed in the mid-1980s and replaced by John Giblin, who debuted at Live Aid in 1985. “Street Fighting Years” (1989) topped the UK chart despite Gaynor and Giblin leaving mid-session, and keyboardist Mick MacNeil quit at the close of the subsequent tour. “Real Life” (1991) and “Good News from the Next World” (1995) followed as the band’s lineup narrowed to the core of Kerr and Burchill, with Forbes and Gaynor rejoining in 1996 and 1997 respectively. “Neapolis” (1998) was the band’s only album released through Chrysalis Records. By the time of “Neon Lights” (2001), the band had regrouped around Kerr, Burchill and new recruit Gordy Goudie, who remains in the lineup today. “Cry” followed in 2002, backed by the band’s first North American tour in seven years. Simple Minds went on to release “Black & White 050505” (2005), “Graffiti Soul” (2009), which gave the band its first UK top 10 album in 14 years, “Big Music” (2014), “Acoustic” (2016), “Walk Between Worlds” (2018) and “Direction of the Heart” (2022) through BMG. The band’s catalogue has topped 60 million albums sold worldwide, and its accolades include the 2016 Ivor Novello Award for Outstanding Song Collection and the 2014 Q Inspiration Award. The current lineup pairs founders Kerr and Burchill with Goudie, Sarah Brown, Ged Grimes, Cherisse Osei and Erik Ljunggren; in September 2026 the band announced a new studio album, “Sacrosanct”, due for release on 29 January 2027. Twenty-five years after “Neon Lights”, the covers album remains the clearest record of the influences, from Kraftwerk to Joy Division, that shaped the band’s own sound.

items.body: Silence has a talent for passing itself off as peace. Two people can share a room, exchange the necessary pleasantries, and conduct an entire argument without troubling the air between them. Inside, every withheld accusation is already gathering speed. Given enough time, even “How was your day?” can begin to sound like a contact sport. Milan quartet October take that condition onto the ice in their video for Universe. The fourth single from their debut album, Dancing Like an Idiot, out now through Waddafuzz! Records, follows the uncomfortable distance between what a relationship looks like from the outside and what its participants are putting themselves through within it. A frozen surface can conceal considerable commotion, and October have enlisted a hockey team to give those private collisions a public airing. The song itself has a supple, sophisticated swing. A rhythmic bassline brings the new wave funk of Roxy Music and Japan to mind, its firm articulation keeping the groove grounded as sustained guitar tones stretch above it. The snare lands at deliberate intervals, leaving generous space around each strike. There is a progressive streak in the arrangement, a willingness to let the instrumental passages stretch and change shape without losing the underlying rhythm. Gianluca Villa sings in a silky upper register reminiscent of Peter Gabriel, his measured delivery building to increasingly impassioned peaks on the line “A Message from the stars.” A gentle guitar jangle carries the song forward, lifting some of its emotional weight. A string interlude zigzags through the arrangement as the vocal rises into a high croon, and tension builds until the full force of the performance comes crashing back. Directed and edited by Fabrizio Grasso, with concept and production by Davide Debenedetti for Filmico, the video makes that division visible. October perform on the rink beneath bright backlights, framed against rows of empty seats, while members of Sgularat Hockey Club Milano skate around them in yellow and black. The musicians hold their positions as the players accelerate, compete, and cut across the space between them. Pads, helmets, and sticks give anger and frustration a physical vocabulary; the ice supplies the emotional temperature. There is something both funny and painfully apt about bringing protective equipment into a love song. Here, the action surrounding the band becomes the argument nobody is having aloud: misunderstandings, thwarted attempts at connection, and the helplessness of trying to reach someone who has become difficult to recognise. Grasso lets the rink carry the metaphor, its broad white expanse accommodating all that activity without offering much warmth. Watch the video for Universe below: October formed in Milan in 2024, bringing together musicians whose backgrounds include Grandi Animali Marini, Il Fieno, NOA, and Egokid, alongside collaborations with Veracrash and I Ministri. Villa handles guitar and vocals, joined by bassist Dario Giordano, drummer Paolo Soffientini, and synth player Davide “dEbE” Debenedetti. Their debut was recorded at Casamedusa with Francesco Campanozzi and Frigo Studio with Francesco Ferrari, then mixed and mastered by Paolo Mauri. Released on March 30, 2026, Dancing Like an Idiot is available digitally and on vinyl. Listen to Universe below and order the album here. items.body: There is a particular kind of youthful ambition that treats a synthesizer’s limitations as somebody else’s problem. If the arrangement feels crowded, another drum track might settle the argument; if the equipment begins to struggle, perhaps it needs to be programmed harder. Baltimore’s Pygmy Children remember their earliest recordings with the affectionate candor of two people who have since learned exactly what they were putting their machines through. More than thirty years later, those experiments are getting a fresh listen. Out now through Re:Mission Entertainment, Malignant: Redux revisits the electro-industrial duo’s 1994 debut album, Malignant, and the preceding 1993 EP, Facedown. Released October 2, the collection brings brothers Pete and Brian Roper back to the recordings that introduced them to the American industrial underground, with the digital edition collecting both releases in full. Originally recorded at Hit and Run Studios in Rockville, Maryland, with engineer Steve Carr, the material has received its first official remaster from Jeff Mortimer at JM Mastering. Brian Roper supplies the Redux artwork, completing a return to a period when the duo’s appetite for dense arrangements regularly outpaced the resources at their disposal. The brothers describe those sessions with refreshing frankness: “Admittedly, the record sounds pretty raw. We were novices trying to create something multi-layered and frenetic, working with what we had and probably not fully knowing what the hell we were doing, just going for it. Some of the synths were being pushed to the point of voice exhaustion, while multiple drum tracks pounded away simultaneously. Looking back, some editing was probably in order, but the intention was always there. We may not have hit the target exactly, but the aim was definitely there.” That willingness to admit the excess is part of the appeal. Their account describes two musicians learning through accumulation, pursuing an idea until the equipment itself began to object. The early titles suggest a similarly restless approach: Core moves between Resistance and Meltdown, while Facedown appears in Reflex, Manic, Bootstamp, and Dead versions across the digital collection. Even the track listing seems reluctant to leave an experiment alone. For Re:Mission founder Wes Turner, the release also carries a personal connection. Pygmy Children helped shape his taste in dark electronic music during the 1990s; three decades on, his label is releasing both their new work and these formative recordings. Turner now gets to put the records that helped educate him back into other listeners’ hands. Listen to Malignant : Redux below: Malignant : Redux by Pygmy Children Pygmy Children first surfaced with Facedown on Noname/Noslogan Productions, following it with Malignant before moving on to Deconstruct, released by Cleopatra in 1995, and Low Life Dream, issued through Sub/Mission Records and Out Of Line in 1998. After years away, the brothers returned in 2025 through Re:Mission with Coincidental Strategies, accompanied by singles including I Have No Name and Signal Unknown. Their recent single Proof in Lies, which we covered in August, leads their forthcoming fifth studio album, Into The Silence. With new material underway, Malignant : Redux offers a timely return to the duo’s beginnings. The brothers can now afford to smile at their early excesses, though the synthesizers they used back then may still be entitled to an apology. Malignant : Redux is available digitally and on CD via Re:Mission Entertainment. Order here or find additional listening options here. Digital edition: Both Malignant and Facedown in full, comprising 16 tracks. Limited digipak CD: An edition of 100 copies, containing Malignant plus Fear, the B-side from the Facedown EP, with the digital edition included. Three-CD autographed bundle: Malignant : Redux alongside autographed original pressings of Malignant and Facedown, plus the digital edition. Limited to 25 bundles, with US shipping only. items.body: 2026.10.08 東京交響楽団2027/28シーズンラインナップ発表記者会見が開催！ 2年目は「危険な年」？ 2026年10月7日、ミューザ川崎シンフォニーホールで行なわれた東京交響楽団の2027／28シーズンラインナップ発表記者会見に、音楽監督ロレンツォ・ヴィオッティが登壇した。 2026／27シーズンから音楽監督に就任し、その任期が2034年3月までの延長が発表されたばかりのヴィオッティ。「まだこの第1シーズンの最中にはありますが、もうすでに楽団員はもちろんのこと、スタッフ、そして合唱団、すべての方々を私は心から誇りに思っています」と切り出した。 その実感を強くしたのが、9月に演奏したフランツ・シュミット《七つの封印の書》だった。「本当に素晴らしい演奏をしてくれました。特に合唱団は、あたかも簡単な作品であるかのように演奏してくれました。でも、実際にはもっとも難しいと言っていい作品です」。 そんな現在地から、2027／28シーズンにさらに大きな挑戦となるのが演奏会形式で上演するワーグナーの《ローエングリン》だ。「ステージのないワーグナー作品というのは、一見難しいように思われますが、《ローエングリン》は、皆さんがちょっと目をつぶって、音楽に耳を傾けていただければ、その情景の動きをありありと思い浮かべることができるオペラの一つではないかと思っています」。 シュミット作品のみならず、ヴェルディやブラームスのレクイエムを経て挑むワーグナーは、「これまで積み重ねてきた経験がすべて大きく実って、それがつながっていく作品」だと語った。 ロレンツォ・ヴィオッティ 1990年スイス・ローザンヌ出身。カダケス国際指揮者コンクール、ライプツィヒMDR指揮者コンクールなどで優勝し、2015年ザルツブルク音楽祭にてネスレ・ヤング・コンダクター賞を受賞。グルベンキアン管弦楽団首席指揮者（2018～2021）、ネーデルラント・フィルハーモニー管弦楽団およびオランダ国立歌劇場首席指揮者（2021～2025）を歴任。これまでにウィーン・フィル、ベルリン・フィル、ロイヤル・コンセルトヘボウ管、ライプツィヒ・ゲヴァントハウス管、ベルリン・シュターツカペレ、ミュンヘン・フィル、ロサンゼルス・フィル、クリーヴランド管などを指揮。オペラにおいてもウィーン国立歌劇場、パリ・オペラ座、ミラノ・スカラ座などに客演し、高い評価を得ている。 2014年、東京交響楽団との共演で日本デビュー。初共演から10年を迎えた2024年８月、東京交響楽団次期音楽監督に任命され、2026/27シーズンより第4代音楽監督に就任。2028年8月からはチューリッヒ歌劇場音楽総監督に就任する。 ©︎N.Ikegami また、音楽監督2年目にあたる来シーズンについては、「2年目こそ、ある意味での脆さが出やすい、危険性をはらんだ年になります。しかし、少しずつ相手のことがわかり始めると、当然ながら“小さなぶつかり”も出てくる。実はこれはこれで大切なことだと私は思っています」と述べた。 「私の任期も3年から8年へと延びました。長くいると、もっともっと音楽を掘り下げ、より高い質と、より多く、広く、深くということが可能になってくると思っています。これからの8年をかけて、できることすべてをする気持ちでいます。より強く、よりよい関係を築いていきたい」と力を込めた。 マーラー、ストラヴィンスキー、シューマンともっと音楽を深く掘る その関係を築いていくために、具体的にはどのようなプログラムが組まれるのか。ヴィオッティが会見で特に注目したのは、マーラー、ストラヴィンスキー、そしてシューマンだった。 今シーズンにすでに演奏したマーラーの交響曲第1番は、「新しい世界の幕開けを思わせる」作品。「本当にその、非常に音楽に対する献身と想像力、そして思い切り、すべてが求められる作品です」。そして来シーズンには交響曲第7番をとりあげる。マーラーが作曲において「和声や作曲技法において挑戦した作品と言える。技術的にも決して簡単ではない」と、オーケストラにとっても大きな挑戦になることを明かした。 そしてストラヴィンスキーについては「私の心にもっとも近い作曲家の一人で、その音色の探求を、東京交響楽団とともにできることを楽しみにしております」と期待を込めた。 最後に、シーズン終盤に置かれるのがシューマンだ。「数週間前に『今、もっとも心にある作曲家は？』と質問されて、シューマンと答えました」。ヴィオッティにとってシューマンは、重くなりすぎてもいけない。一方で、古典的に軽くなりすぎてもいけないそう。「このバランスをオーケストラとともに模索していくことが一つの課題になると思っています」。 来シーズンのイメージカラーと同じバーガンディ色のセーターをお召しのヴィオッティ監督 ヴァイオリニストの佐藤俊介がクリエイティブ・パートナーに 2027年4月から3年間、ヴァイオリニストの佐藤俊介が東京交響楽団クリエイティブ・パートナーに就任することも発表されている。ヴィオッティはまだ直接会ったことはないが、オランダのオーケストラで楽団員から話を聞き、SpotifyやYouTubeなどで彼の演奏を聴いているという。 「非常に好印象を抱いています。オーケストラとしても、室内楽的に、お互いに親密によく聴き合う姿勢は、とても大事なんです。そのような意味でも彼を迎えるのは大きな意味を持つと思っています」 廣岡楽団長からは、佐藤との活動を通して、指揮者を置かずに一緒に演奏するような取り組みや、バロック音楽のアプローチ、さらにはこれまでオーケストラが取り組んでこなかったジャンルとのコラボレーションへの期待も語られた。 items.body: 『声なき声のドローイング:スキャン画像』2026［© Shu Yonezawa, Courtesy of SNOW Contemporary］ 会期：2026/07/17～2026/09/05 会場：SNOW Contemporary［東京都］ 公式サイト：http://snowcontemporary.com/exhibition/202607.html （前編から） ステートメントには続けて「彩度は低く細かな色相の差異で描いたのはキャラクターと捉えるには薄く複雑な声未満の存在であ」ったと書かれている。米澤は以前から、キャラクターの「声」に関心を寄せてきた。実際、キャラクターのアイデンティティを規定するうえで声はイメージと同等以上に重要な役割を果たしているだろう。しかし米澤が声に見出しているのは、もっと広い可能性であるようにも思われる──アニマとキャラクターのあいだを自由に往還する現象としての可能性を。 そもそも“anima”が「魂」と同時に「息」や「風」を意味する語であったことを思い出そう。 神が息を吹き込むこと （ インスピレーション ） によって事物はアニメートされる。世界を巡る空気の流れが振動としてあらわれたものが声だと考えるなら、それはまさにアニマをもっとも色濃く反映した現象だと言えるだろう。無論、この魂-呼吸-声といった直線的な繋がりは、あくまでも西欧的な生命観にもとづくものであることに注意しなければならない。例えばアーティストの布施琳太郎は、米澤が描く「オバケ」状のキャラクターにおいてしばしば口が身体（構造）から遊離していることを指摘し、ここにアニマと声のより自由な関係の可能性を見ている★3。すなわち、ヤツメウナギなどに代表される無顎類が摂食のための口と呼吸のための鰓を完全に独立して発達させたように、米澤のキャラクター表現は、私たちが生物学的な人体構造によって規定されているがゆえに硬直してしまったアニマとの関係性を、いまひとたびときほぐすことを試みているのではないか、と★4。 自由に泳ぎ回る口があらゆる場所で開き、声を発する。もはやこのとき、「口」を画面内に描かれた身体パーツのみに限定する理由はない。むしろ米澤作品はつねに「口」そのものとともに存在してきたとも言えるだろう——フレームという口として。キャンバス、トレーシングペーパー、ビニール、モニタ、スクリーン——手法や素材の別によらず、米澤の作品は基本的に矩形の画面を前提としているように見える。特に本展では、これまでビニール自体をピンで固定する形式を主としてきた「アニマの通り跡」シリーズがアルミフレームに張られ、壁や空中に吊られている。また、映像を主とするインスタレーション的な作品《別の海としての身体》では、小型のモニタが半透明のアクリルケースによってさらにフレーミングされ、スピーカー——もっとも象徴的な機械の口——だけが隣接する壁面にさまよい出ている。とはいえ、アニメーション表現を背景に持つ米澤が矩形のフレームを意識するのは当然のことであり、そうした強固な枠があればこそ、不定形に蠢くアニマたちの流出もまた強調されるのだ、と言うことはできるだろう。ではその上で、あらゆる場所に開かれるフレームを「口」とみなすことはどんな意味を持つのか。 ［撮影：木奥惠三］ そもそも人間の発生に限ってみても、口とは「顔に開いた穴」などではない。妊娠初期にあたる8週から12週ごろ、胎児の顔部では、周囲から伸び上がってきた突起が中央で癒合することによって口唇や口蓋がつくられ、口の輪郭が完成する。口とはほんらい、開くものではなく、意図的に閉じ損なったものなのだ。最初はすべてが穴であり、その穴が埋められていく過程で残された残余としてのみ、口は定義しうる。ここで、白川静が「口」という漢字の成り立ちについて唱えた次のような説が思い出される。いわく、口は人間の開いた口唇ではなく、祝詞をおさめる器（サイ）のかたちに由来するのだと。学問的な信憑性に疑問はあるものの、解釈としては興味深い。すなわち、口を漢字練習帳のマス目のような「文字の到来を待つ空白」そのものの象形として捉えるなら、それは「いまだ閉じられていないこと」それ自体を意味する。そしてその「閉じられていない」という事実こそが、声を召喚する。口が声を発するのではない。むしろあらかじめ世界に満ちているそれが、たまたま口が見出されたときに受信され、声としてあらわれるのだ。この意味において、世界のあちこちに口を見出すことはそのまま声を見出すことであり、米澤が言うところの「アニメーション」概念のもっとも素朴なかたちであるように思える★5。 最後に、広義の「口」の観点から、米澤の代表的なモチーフである目についても考えておこう。目の本質を眼球ではなく、それが収まる眼窩やまぶたといった立体的なフレームに置いてみると、そこにはひとつの水槽のようなものが浮かび上がってくる。眼球というアニマが泳ぐ、涙で満たされた水槽が。口が開閉するように、目はまばたきを行なう。まばたきは視界を寸断して不完全な視覚をつくり出すが、同時に眼球を涙液でコーティングし、目を開き続けることで生じる像のブレを修正してもいる。つまり、視覚をいくつものフレームに分割する行為によってこそ、眼球はかろうじて息をしている。まばたきとは、目に許されたただひとつの呼吸であり、同時にこの器官が「閉じ損ねている」ことの証でもある。では果たして、完全な視界＝ずっと目を開き続ける視界などというものはありえるのだろうか。もしありえるのならばそのとき、一体なにが見えるのだろうか。 ［撮影：木奥惠三］ ここまでの議論をふまえると、本展は展示室に開いた口から流れ込んだアニマたちが、室内のあちらこちらに思い思いの像をあらわしていくひとつの現象として捉えられる——その構造はさながら、写真機の原型としての「 暗い部屋 （ カメラ・オブスキュラ ） 」を思わせる。しかし冒頭で述べたとおり、本展はむしろ光で満たされた「明るい部屋」としてあらわれている。ただしそれは、事物の輪郭を切り分ける乾いた光ではなく、目を凝らすほどにそのイメージを滲ませる湿った光、水底で感じる明るさに近い。波間でゆらぎ、水を透過して散乱した光が絶えず私たちの目を幻惑する。言葉遊びを許すなら「 水妖の部屋 （ カメラ・オブ・スキュラ ） 」とでも言えようか。水妖&efDotアニマは気ままに水と光の中に溶けてまわり、そのゆらめきのあいだに身を翻す。あちこちで口が開いては何ごとかをつぶやき、また消え去っていく。私の口もそれにつられて開くのだが、ごぼごぼと水音を立てるばかりで上手く喋れない。いや、そこでは私の口を借りて水妖たちの声があらわれているのだ。私がまだその声を捉えることができないというだけで。ぱくぱくと単調に開閉を繰り返すだけの口の動きは、再生か逆再生かを区別できない。それゆえに、時間は渦を巻いてほどけていく。水に包まれた私の目はまばたきを忘れ、ただ見開かれている。 ★3──布施琳太郎「無顎類のアニマ：キャラクターアートの終焉の後で」（米澤柊『泳ぐ目たちのアーカイヴ』所収、2026） ★4──私たち人間を思わせる身体パーツや骨格構造をところどころに有しつつも、中心性は不確かで、不定形に広がっている──こうした米澤作品におけるキャラクターの比喩として、私がまっさきに思いついたのはホヤであった。ホヤは尾索動物に属し、私たち脊椎動物と比較的近縁の生物である。オタマジャクシ型の幼生時は脳や脊索を備え、遊泳しながら住処を探す。この時点では摂食を行なわないため口はなく（眼点や嗅覚細胞の原型は存在するものの）器官としての目や鼻もない。そして無事、岩などを見つけるとそこに固着し、よく知られたホヤの形になる。脳や脊索、眼点を失う代わりに大きな口が開き、水を漉し取って栄養を摂取するだけの存在となる。いわばホヤは、脊椎動物的な身体構造を幼生から成体までのタイムスケールのなかに散在させている生物として捉えられる。言い換えれば、ホヤを時間的に再構成したものとして人間を考えることもできるだろう。 ★5──ここまで見てきた要素をまとめると、米澤の作品は、暗黙化した身体感覚／構造を再構成することを通じて、私たちが不可知化してしまったアニマを汲み上げようとしているのだといえる。そこには目（視覚）や声（聴覚）に加え、手指のモチーフを通じた触覚的なイメージや、米澤が「イメージの骨／アニメーションの骨」といった言い回しで示唆する、抽象的な身体感覚なども含まれている。しかし、嗅覚的な要素に限ってはあまり読み取れない。そもそも、米澤の描くキャラクター表象において鼻の存在感はきわめて希薄だ。横顔においてわずかに隆起らしきものが確認できるが、正面顔では鼻、とりわけ鼻孔はほぼ捨象されている。鼻は脊椎動物に特有の器官であり、もともと大脳は嗅覚情報処理のために大きく発達したのだとも言われている。 鑑賞日：2026/07/25（土）

items.body: 『声なき声のドローイング:スキャン画像』2026［© Shu Yonezawa, Courtesy of SNOW Contemporary］ 会期：2026/07/17～2026/09/05 会場：SNOW Contemporary［東京都］ 公式サイト：http://snowcontemporary.com/exhibition/202607.html 「声なき声のキャラクター」は米澤柊による個展である。展示作品はすべて2026年の新作で、なかでも米澤がここ一年ほど取り組んでいるという油絵作品が全体の七割近くを占めている。画面はどれも彩度の低い色が細かく重ねられることで構成されており、その茫洋とした色彩の渦を眺めるうちに、人間めいた輪郭や骨格、目、手の残像といったものたちの印象がかろうじて浮かび上がってくる。これは直感的には、白飛びした視界を思わせた。眠りから醒めたときに誰しもが味わうように、暗がりから急に光に満ちた空間へと晒された視界は明順応が間に合わず白く飽和する。そしてそこから徐々に、事物の輪郭や色彩を取り戻していく。しかし本展において、その視界が完全に明瞭になることはない。作品のあいだを行き交うにしたがい、眼球を包む涙液そのものが白濁していくかのごとく、乳白色の闇がゆるやかに立ち込める。六本木の雑居ビルの薄暗がりを切り開いてあらわれる端正なホワイトキューブともあいまって、本展はどこまでも明るく、しかし──それゆえに──知覚の不完全性を露わにしている。では、そんな淡い光の中に漂っているものたちとは一体なんなのだろうか。 ［撮影：木奥惠三］ 繰り返し述べられてきた内容のため簡潔に触れるにとどめるが、多くの手法やメディウムを横断した米澤の制作には「アニマ（魂・生命性）」への関心が通底しており、とりわけ特徴的なのが「オバケ」への着目である。「オバケ」とはアニメーション制作において、あるフレームとフレームのあいだの動きを補完し、物体の動きをより活き活きとみせるためにあえて（静止画としては）崩れた描写を行なう技術を指す。実際、現時点における米澤作品のもっとも一般的なイメージとは、身体がほどけて散らばりつつあるかのような「オバケ」としてのキャラクターたちの図像だろう。 画面内の事物を 息づかせ （ アニメートす ） るための技術が「オバケ」と呼ばれる逆説──いや、考えてみれば逆説ではないのだ。さまざまなアニメ作品において、「オバケ」のコマを単体で切り取ったスクリーンショットは作画崩壊の事例としてネットミーム化してきた。これはアニメーションの中割り技術への無知から生じた誤認にすぎないわけだが、ではなぜ人々が「オバケ」に対してそれほど強烈な印象を共有しえたのかといえば、なめらかなアニメーションのなかに「見てはいけないものを見てしまった」と感じたからにほかならないだろう。すなわち、「オバケ」とはアニメーションの物語時間を補填するために見逃され続けることを運命付けられた存在であり、それゆえ、ひとたび意識に上ったその姿は本物の怪異さながらに「ぞっとする」ものとなるのだ。 画面内におけるキャラクターの自律性が担保されるためには、無数の崩れかけた非-自律的な なにものか ・・・・・ が不可欠であるというジレンマ。米澤はこの主従──アニメーションを規定する所与の時間と、それを埋め合わせる「オバケ」という関係性──を撹乱する。ほんらい見てはいけないものである「オバケ」を一枚の図像──しかもモニタやキャンバスといったいかにも「見るべき」質感を帯びたもの──として固定したうえで、その身体の崩壊を過剰に押し進めていく。そのとき、アニメーションのなめらかさを整えるパテのごとき不定形な「オバケ」はフレームの隙間から這い出して、別の時間的秩序を育み始める──フレームレートに従って生起する単線的な物語とは異なる時間を。そこでは過去や未来は等しくまなざされ、因果もまた意味を失う。米澤はそうして、フレームとフレームのあいだの飛躍を補完するためにのみ生を許された存在に、 別種の生の可能性 （ アニマ ） を見ようとするわけだ。 このようにアニメーションをひとつの基点とする米澤の作品群は、その手法にかかわらず複雑な層性を帯びてきた。例えば米澤の代表的なシリーズである「オバケのスクリーンショット」では、現実の風景写真のなかに「オバケ」としてのキャラクターたちが描き込まれている。レイヤーの集合としてのデジタルペイントが現実の風景に重ね合わされ、しかもそれは連続する無数のフレームの一瞬を捉えた「スクリーンショット」として位置付けられる。こうした時間的・空間的な複層性のなかをたゆたう米澤の作品は、必然的に「いま・ここ」からの遊離を予感させる。イメージは確かに目の前に存在するはずなのに、どこかヴェールに包まれているような捉えどころのなさがついてまわる。それは失われたものへの憧憬なのか、来たるべきものの予兆なのか──無論、どちらでもありうる。先に述べたとおり、米澤が紡ごうとする非線形の時間的秩序のなかにおいて、過去・現在・未来は等価に立ち並んでいるのだから★1。アニマはつねに、現前と予感のあいだで見え隠れする。 この観点において、描画面をレイヤー状に切り分けるためのアナログな技術として油絵を位置付けることも可能だろう。しかし当然ながら、油絵においては絵具の乾燥状態が層を決定する。乾ききる前に次のストロークを置けば下の層は物理的に巻き込まれ、層と層の境界——それは時間的秩序そのものと言ってもいい——が相互に浸潤可能となる（もちろん、実際に米澤がそのような描法を用いたかどうかは問題ではない）。ここで層を決定しているのは描き手の意志ではなく、絵具の乾燥速度、すなわちメディウムに固有の時間である。フレームとフレームを繋ぐフラットな時間のあいだから、「オバケ」が棲まう異なる時間が這い出していったように、ここでは層と層のあいだにメディウム由来の液体的な時間感覚が流れ込んでいる★2。 ［撮影：斉藤桃加］ 本展のステートメント冒頭には「かたちを選んで描こうとするほど選ばなかったものを切りすててしまうようで息苦しく、絵は段々と白くなっていった」とある。幾重にもゆらぎながら仄かに浮かび上がる油彩のイメージは、さまざまな連想を喚起する。例えば長時間露光による写真。そこでは被写体が動くことによって輪郭がブレ、イメージは次第に発散へと向かっていく。あるいは拡散モデルにおける画像生成（を開始まもなく停止させたようす）。ここでは反対に、ブレの極点とでもいうべきノイズのなかに任意の輪郭が幻視され、イメージが浮かび上がってくる。輪郭が浮かび上がる前のさざめきと、輪郭が溶け去っていった後の残響。米澤の画面が置かれているのは、まさにその異なる二つのベクトルが調停され、判定が無化される地点／時点である。 米澤は「世界が意味になる前の複雑さについて考えたい」という。しかしここまで見てきたように「ほんらいの複雑な世界が、人間の手による記号的分節によって単純化されてしまう」という単線的な因果とは別の場所に向けてこそ、米澤の作品はひらかれているように思える。そういえば、私が米澤の油絵の画面からはじめに想起したもの。それは写真でもAIでもなく、ほとんど面影だけになってしまった記憶のことであった。限界まで薄れ抽象化された記憶は、それがどこに属するのかをもはや判別できず、ゆえに時間のあいだを自由に飛び回り、私たちの認識に影響を及ぼして回る。はじめて見たはずのものをなぜか懐かしく思うこと。反対に、何度も見たはずのものをなぜだか瑞々しく感じること。そうした認識の脱臼ともいうべき瞬間を真に受けて生き続けることが、可能であるように思えるのだ。米澤の作品世界においてならば。 ★1──個人的にここで想起するのは小林泰三「酔歩する男」である。作中では、一風変わったタイムトラベルの方法が描かれる。登場人物は「時間とは本来非連続なものであり、そこに連続性を見出しているのは私たちの脳である」との仮説を示し、実際に脳内の時間感覚を司る部位を破壊することで、さまざまな時間点をランダムに飛び回る存在となる。それは過去と未来が等しく可能性のなかに溶け込んだ非線形の人生であり、そこには始まりも終わりもありえない。 ★2──ここで思い出すのは、ジェフ・ウォールによるエッセイ「Photography and Liquid Intelligence」（1989）である。ウォールは、写真を織りなす光学と液体の緊張関係に焦点を当てた。つまりカメラという緻密な機械が生産する写真は、最終的に現像という液体の不確定性に晒されることで顕現するのであり、ウォールはここに乾いた近代的知性のオルタナティブとしての湿った知性、液体的知性を見るのである。エッセイはこの液体的知性をソラリスの海に喩えることで結ばれる。観測者の記憶からイメージを汲み出し反射させるその海には、結ばれる前のあらゆるイメージの素がたゆたいながら、こちらを見返しているわけだ。写真とは、現像液に潜む無数のイメージのひとつをたまさか拾い上げたものにすぎず、もう一度現像し直せばそこにはまったく違ったイメージが掬い取られるのかもしれない。フィルムを現像液に浸し続ければ、その還元力はやがて感光していない臭化銀にまで至り、あらゆるイメージを黒く塗りつぶしていく。それは白く飽和した油彩のイメージと対になるものだろう。 （後編へ） 鑑賞日：2026/07/25（土）

items.excerpt: Over the past five years, Philip Samartzis has been building a body of distinct work. items.body: Over the past five years, Philip Samartzis has been building a body of distinct work. The interrelated recordings are identifiable by their adjacent titles: 2021’s Polar Force / Array (with Eugene Ughetti); 2023’s Atmospheres and Disturbances; 2024’s Air Pressure (with Michael Vorfeld); and now 2026’s Atmospheric Pressure, again with Vorfeld. The starting point for these ventures was a pair of residencies sponsored by the Australian Antarctic Territory Arts Fellowship program. Samartzis was able to capture some incredible recordings in sub-zero temperatures, and they have proven to be a wealth of material in both pure and sculpted forms. As on Air Pressure, Samartzis contributes electronics, Vorfeld stringed instruments and percussion. The new set zeroes in on a 36-hour blizzard at the Casey Research Station in 2016. Amid the hundred-knot winds and white-out conditions, “the station was reduced to pressure, vibration, and sound.” Simply picturing David Nielson’s cover image of David Ward inspecting dog lines in 1990, one can already feel the cold and intuit the level of difficulty. “Gravitational Overflow” sets the stage with slowly increasing winds and the creak of vanes (personified by Vorfeld’s instruments). The wind and snow create their own music, an undulating drone of literal white noise. Percussion enters as sympathetic partner; one imagines the rattling of glass and iron, caught in a maelstrom of Biblical proportions. Toward the end, these metallic pats and taps take center stage, as if representing the eye of the hurricane. “Depression” refers to atmospheric conditions, although one would be forgiven for thinking that it might mirror a mood. The isolation of research stations often produces feelings of malaise. The electronics and radio chatter are surprises in the wake of the opener; some portions even sound like turntable scratches or graffiti cans being shaken. The focus is not on the machine hum and motor sputter, but instead, what happens when the electricity fails. The purely percussive section arrives earlier, in the sixth minute, like the last sounds of a man caught in a storm, having lost all bearings, facing death by making music one last time, his only audience the abyss. “Cold Front” reveals the full depth of the danger. The strings seem as agitated as the snow, the percussion as frozen as the sleet, the electronics as charged as the air. Sound bends around the cymbals like sheets of ice. In the sixth minute, a sound like clomping hooves comes across like a phantasm. The actual storm mixes with the impression of the storm to convey feelings of being trapped inside or wandering outside: stir crazy or snow-blind. The applause at the very end is well-earned. We’re not sure how many more Antarctic recordings Samartzis has in the bag, but as so few of us are likely to hear them in person, each release arrives as a revelation. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Rather than resolving its strange machinery, Noxi Melank leaves it in motion—a collection of damaged systems, unstable rhythms, and modular forms continually finding new ways to become something else. Blurry to the senses, roughened around the edges Noxi Melank by ignatius   One of our favorite crafters of modular abstraction, glitch, and electronic noise, Ignatius (Buried In Time) makes a striking debut with Noxi Melank for Evel. Across eight pieces, sound worlds are explored, eroded, fragmented, and reshaped from start to finish. A surreal, broken rhythmic transition opens the nearly 10-minute opus “IdleDeep,” where blips, bleeps, echoes, scattered voices, and subdued electronic residue flicker beneath a slippery surface of decay. “GenderLimo” picks up the pace, remaining subtle, melankolic, and abstract as drifting, crumpled tones and drones take shape. Its sounds feel almost timeless, like abandoned and dented machines searching for somewhere to restart, mutate, and build unfamiliar worlds. As Ignatius’ glitch language unfolds piece by piece, each movement is marked by an unusually astute clarity within the noise. “Editorial,” for instance, reveals itself through Autechre meets Syl Kougaï-infused rhythmic deformation and energy, where modular structures seem to buckle, reconfigure, and find new momentum. While low-end rattling soundscapes provide a constant benchmark for Noxi Melank, Ignatius finds particular comfort in unusual time signatures—blurry to the senses, roughened around the edges, yet always moving forward with the precision of a practiced sound sculptor. Translucent structures of decay and erosion :: As the album persists, its tracks remain connected through an elusive, surreal logic. “Nonsequitirs” and “Locations” are especially revealing, unfolding as downtempo, almost translucent electroacoustic structures of decay and erosion. Dark passages maneuver through electronic debris, allowing fragments of rhythm and texture to surface before disappearing again. Closing with “SloxiEnds,” Ignatius shifts toward a more upbeat final chapter. Its Tri Repetae-like abstraction carries an unexpected sense of beauty, gradually transforming through layers of modular distortion—something the cover art depicts with uncanny precision—before arriving at an almost Eastern-sounding flourish. Rather than resolving its strange machinery, Noxi Melank leaves it in motion—a collection of damaged systems, unstable rhythms, and modular forms continually finding new ways to become something else. Noxi Melank is available on Evel. [Bandcamp] Noxi Melank by ignatiusThe post Ignatius :: Noxi Melank (Evel) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

Economy of Movement arrives as five cuts of seriously diverse breakbeat chicaner
items.body: With Economy of Movement, Antipodean breakbeat pioneer Social Sport delivers five restless, shape-shifting cuts where fractured rhythms, heavyweight bass and psychedelic atmospheres turn the breakbeat tradition into something fiercely alive and forward-moving. Five cuts of seriously diverse breakbeat chicanery Economy of Movement by Social Sport   Antipodean breakbeat pioneer Social Sport knows what time it is. Economy of Movement arrives as five cuts of seriously diverse breakbeat chicanery, ranging across the territory occupied by beats that have escaped the tyranny of the 1 and 3. Because that, essentially, is the point: breakbeat breaks the line. Kicks bounce and lurch, snares and claps shuffle, hi-hats stammer and skitter, creating pace, tension and the possibility of movement in the spaces between expectation. Mr Sport understands these theatrics and deploys them with integrity and valor, honoring the traditions and foundations through which creator, creativity and the creative œuvre continually collide. “Inflow” opens with serious intent. Kicks move through silver atmospheres of mountain mist and textural haze, summoning elemental forces and earthly gravitas. “Life” then takes the Amen break on a tangential excursion, all aplomb and swagger, building rolling thunder from didgeridoos and chopped vocal commands. There’s something here that, to my ears at least, accidentally invokes the gods of FSOL’s “Papua New Guinea.” Not pastiche. Not homage. Something more interesting: an apparently necessary Occidental parallel evolution. Grit and grift rendered kinetic :: “Movement Economy” introduces stop-start rhythms and female vocal fragments into a 2-step-adjacent landscape of spring-loaded didges and ticking-time-bomb mood swings. Dark? Perhaps. But I don’t really read darkness here as darkness. I read power. Necessity. Seriousness. Grit and grift rendered kinetic. Tight and sick as one. “Still Working On It” brings the archetypal breakbeat throwdown: reverbed 303, filtering synth tapestries and enough dancefloor adjacency to make the whole thing twitch. It’s a proper closer, exiting with a kablamo and the brand-new stallion hoofs of badassery. Then LOIF gets involved, reworking the title track by diving beneath its surface and finding more room in the apparent darkness. The bottom end comes forward, the drums sharpen, and the bass assumes a more pronounced riff-like presence. Above it, silver clouds of smog and illumination hover while acid swirls stripe the walls with psychedelic color. It’s a redub, a reroute and a conversation with the original. More importantly, it completes the circle: five tracks that collectively reveal the specificity of an artist’s particular lens, and the possibilities that emerge when movement is allowed to escape its economy. From the other side of the globe, I see you.​ Kudos. The work is superb. Economy of Movement is available on Steeplejack. items.body: Trippin’ is timely, the London (Ontario) label cementing the Newfoundland-based producer’s growing profile with a more substantial presence. A rollout spanning a couple of years via teaser and remix releases Trippin' by Zachary Gray   Canadian ambient/electronic practitioner Zachary Gray’s album Trippin’ is set to land on A Person Disguised as People. The 9-track LP comes on the back of the previous Suburbia EP (APDAP, 2024) (see igloo’view) with a rollout spanning a couple of years via teaser and remix releases. Nov. 2024 saw a 2-track taster Trippin’ / In Arrears (igloo’view here) as part of APDAP‘s A/B Series; back then the title track tasted like a ‘a doleful brooder, replete with melodic synth lines recalling early 90s Warp luminaries (cf. Black Dog, Plaid), layers of rhythm and harmony making for an uneasy introspective tenor’ (igloo’view), with ‘a deft touch in blending electronic production detail and filmic affect’ overall commended. Spin-off EP Trippin’ Variations (igloo’view here) followed Feb. 2025, featuring re-thinks of the title track by mates of Gray incl. Hidden Rivers, SXXN, Soft Operator and James Scott. Now comes the full release, somewhat later than planned—Autumn 2026; the Fall that pride came before perhaps! The album furthers the evolution of Gray’s anatomy, tracing years of his musical composition, revision and memory, from a back catalog grounded in early releases such as Under a Red Sky (Synesthesia Media, 2020), Plan B (APDAP, 2020), Hustle Movement (APDAP, 2017), Night Hustle (APDAP, 2016), Containment (APDAP, 2015) plus collabs with luminaries like Benoît Pioulard, Montag, and Sea Oleena. Trippin’ is timely, the London (Ontario) label cementing the Newfoundland-based producer’s growing profile with a more substantial presence. Trippin’ is out on Oct. 9 on A Person Disguised as People. items.body: Mathias Villard is a very promising sound artist and Past Radiance can easily figure among my top favorite albums for this year. Exquisite, wistful, cinematic, alluring and emotionally transportive. For fans of Alessandro Cortini, Bvdub, Loscil, Markus Fjellström and Terence Hannum. Once more, Affin proves to be in the first league concerning modern-day ambient-lush drone music. The album flows like a gigantic oceanic movement Past Radiance by Mathias Villard   Mathias Villard is a French sound artist now based in Düsseldorf, Germany. He is a new face in the world of ambient-drone and orchestral cinematic electronica, but his debut album finds the best possible way to bring it to a larger international audience, thanks to a contract with key indie label Affin (headed by Joachim Spieth). Affin already presents an immense catalog of advanced electronic music with a strong interest in densely layered soundscapes, emotional cinematic escapism and ambient-techno waves. Numerous well-established projects and names are part of the catalogue, among others Pepo Galán and Markus Guentner (with his magnificent Black Dahlia reviewed on Igloo). Past Radiance appears to be a high-class textured ambient release with a strong melodious-moody component that will leave you speechless. If you are fond of lush sonic textures and enveloping electronic sequences sustained by grainy repetitive melodies surrounded by a vast, spacious aura, there is no doubt that this album will reach your heart. The gently sinuous parts and soothing ambiences are powerfully seconded by deep and slowly bassy lines which definitely add more depth and strength to the pieces. Difficult to pick out one piece in particular, as the album flows like a gigantic oceanic movement with rare sonic engulfment. Some lighter moments appear from time to time :: In a track such as “Debris,” this mysterious sonic approach and spacious treatment reach full development: a really massive, cascading and compelling piece. This album integrates a sumptuous sense of motion which meets quite devastating, heart-stirring, almost gloomy but always pleasant melodies. Some lighter moments appear from time to time, as in the curiously pulsating, chilling and bassy “Haze.” The success of this album lies in the meticulously crafted compositional mode but also in the solid technical production. All in all, Mathias Villard is a very promising sound artist and his album can easily figure among my top favorite albums for this year. Exquisite, wistful, cinematic, alluring and emotionally transportive. For fans of Alessandro Cortini, Bvdub, Loscil, Markus Fjellström and Terence Hannum. Once more, this label proves to be in the first league concerning modern-day ambient-lush drone music. Past Radiance is available on Affin. [Bandcamp] The post Mathias Villard :: Past Radiance (Affin) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: New Voices is a new competition for aspiring music critics being launched by The Wire For more than 40 years, The Wire has been publishing writing by a host of original and influential music critics, including Richard Cook, Val Wilmer, Biba Kopf, Ian Penman, Simon Reynolds, Kodwo Eshun, David Keenan, Mark Fisher, Greg Tate, Frances Morgan, Chal Ravens, and many others. The magazine would not exist without a dynamic set of curious, perceptive thinkers and writers. But today, new voices in music writing are being stifled by closing publications, the development of AI, and the fragmentation of local scenes, making it harder than ever for critics to be heard above the noise. Are you an unpublished* writer with ideas about why music, and music criticism, matter – in particular the kind of underground and experimental, uncompromising and provocative music and writing featured in the pages of The Wire? If so, our New Voices competition is a unique opportunity to see your byline in the pages of one of the most renowned and respected music magazines in the world. To enter, submit two original pieces of writing: • A review of a recent album, book, festival, gig, film or exhibition featuring the kind of music you might read about in the pages of The Wire (500 words) • An opinion piece responding to the provocation: “Music criticism is irrelevant in contemporary culture” (500 words) Submit your entries as two separate text-only files, and send them as attachments*, along with your name, email address and a very brief bio, to newvoices@thewire.co.uk. Submissions close at midnight GMT on 7 December 2026. All entries will be read by The Wire’s editorial staff. The winner will be announced, and have their opinion piece published in the March 2027 issue of The Wire. The winner will also receive a £250 cash prize and a free annual digital subscription to the magazine. Three runners up will receive a free annual digital subscription to the magazine. * Terms & conditions: • Entrants should not have had more than three pieces of music writing published and paid for by a third party publication whether in print or online (your own personal blog, Substack etc don’t count). • Submitted entries must not have been previously published elsewhere. • The competition is open to entrants of any age. • Entrants can be based anywhere in the world but should submit their entries in English. • The competition is free to enter. • Only one entry per person – do not send additional material. • Send entries as attachments only, in one of these file formats: .doc, .rtf, or .pdf. Do not send entries as links or Google docs. • The Wire has no obligation to publish the work of any entrants, including the winner, beyond the winning essay. • Entries should discuss music that The Wire would typically cover – adventurous, experimental, DIY, independent, etc. • NB we will not accept entries that have been written, part-written, or polished by AI.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — This group of Finnish Vikings offers a fascinating blend of styles; they look and sound the part during live performances and draw upon Renaissance elements, not only in their compositions but also in the instruments they play. At the same time, they navigate the realm of hard rock with ease, channeling a raw savagery and boundless, spirited energy that permeates their music, extending all the way to the cover art of Susien Y�-Delirium Lupus.Kaisa Saari sings in her native tongue; alongside the distorted guitar, the sounds of a baroque viola and a traditional Viking lyre emerge in "Nostakaamme Malja," while "Muistanko V��rin" showcases Saari's soprano vocal talents. The violin, mandolin, sitar, and accordion infuse sweetness and depth into the raw power of the electric guitar and drums, creating a perfect symbiosis. It concludes like a song from a mystical forest set in the modern age, where classical elements filter through the branches of towering pines to reach a darkness that light would otherwise never penetrate.Kuninkaan Pidot leans more heavily on classical influences; amidst an acoustic soundscape of guitar and violin, it evokes the late-70s folk era of Jethro Tull, until Tarujen Saari shifts toward psychedelia, as if alcohol were flooding that ancient feast for the senses. The lyrics are an adaptation of a very old traditional British ballad known in English as "King Henry." The song highlights that appearances can be deceiving and that generosity, kindness, and genuine courtesy in the face of the unknown are rewarded with great blessings."Musta Sunnuntai" is a beautiful, powerful instrumental that also brings to mind Amon D��l II. There are also moments of relaxed introspection that evoke Scandinavian winters, possessing a cinematic quality ranging from Nordic noir to Bergman films. Armed with violin and accordion, they create a warm atmosphere that melts the snow; what might initially seem cold or aggressive turns tender, like a hearth glowing in the night.The violin arrangements are progressively symphonic in Palatynen laulu, not to mention the accelerated hard rock that also embodies Celtic tradition with electric guitar riffs in Kunungatar Kristiina.Rumpua ly�k�� kuninkaalle proposes a different atmosphere, reminiscent of those slow blues of Janis Joplin and Big Brother & The Holding Company, making it mystical with some jazzy, yet magical, percussion, making Summertime something dense and completely different. Guest musician Jaakko Rajakisto plays the bagpipes on "Hovitanssi." As "Hemminki Ja Tunturin Noita" plays, one cannot help but notice the unstoppable convergence of progressive power and ethnic harmony, embodied by that violin, recalling certain moments from Curved Air; Kaisa Saari channels the energy of Sonja Kristina across the musical spectrum, while the spirit of Daryl Way is present in Marja Tuhkanen.The surprises keep coming, notably the powerful chorus of "Susien Y�", which carries a most welcome Renaissance-style darkness. The ceremony could only culminate in a moment of delicate, subtle, and epic ecstasy, immortalized in the song "W�in�n viikate."

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — The beginning of a new era: the Steve Hogarth era. (Thank you, Darryl Way!)1. "The King of Sunset Town" (8:02) how anyone elevates this band's compositional, instrumental, and sound production skill at the level or even above that of contemporaries IQ, Pendragon, or even Pallas is beyond me! This is so much less! So much prog lite. Steve Hogarth is just one of the rabble when he tries to belt it out like his contemporaries but when he slows it down and expresses from the depths of his delicate soul he is a force to be reckoned with. (13/15)2. "Easter" (5:57) okay music, okay sound production, okay vocal and lyric, corny, simplistic keyboard work; nice drumming, bass, and lead guitar work. (8.75/10)3. "The Uninvited Guest" (3:52) anyone for some BON JOVI? or BRYAN ADAMS? How 'bout some RICHARD MARX? or even Foreigner and latter-day REO Speedwagon or Def Leppard? Here you have it! (8.75/10)4. "Seasons End" (8:07) nice vocal performance by Steve over some weak and saccharine keyboard and guitar arpeggios. The synth washes and piano chords and Pete Trewavas' bass work make it more tolerable. I wish Steve's voice had been mixed more forward/loudly in the final soundscape. In the third minute the sound levels ramp up while Steve H. rests and Steve R. takes over. Nice passage despite the bombastic snare-and-tom rims hits. The sixth minute yields to a whole new motif: one that is founded in glockenspiel pixie dust and other keyboard MIDI sounds meant to emulate dream world scenarios. Another lesson that instructs us as to how one can make much out of very little. (13.5/15)5. "Holloway Girl" (4:27) rotating four-chord keyboard progressions set the stage for this unorthodox Duke "Behind the Lines"-like ballad. (8.75/10)6. "Berlin" (7:43) finally a song construct that is a little more adventurous, a little more nuanced. While there is an undeniable ALAN PARSONS PROJECT sound and feel to this, it has the subtle sophistication of something more poignant, more poetic. I never thought I'd ever be extolling the presence of a saxophone as an enhancing effect but Phil Todd's play here does, in fact, elevate the music to another level. Nice atmospheric passage in the fourth minute to bridge into the song's climactic second half. I do not like Steve R's bottle neck guitar sound but I love Pete Trewavas' bass blasts--and then full-power palette of the sixth minute with Steve H's great list recitation and Steve R.'s excellent rhythm guitar pickings. Very cool! Easily the best two minutes on the album. (13.75/15)7. "After Me" (3:19) � picked 12-string acoustic guitar chords sound a bit like ELP's "Lucky Man" but the chords are different and Steve H's vocal melody lines are quite different--more akin to something from BON JOVI or JOHN COUGAR MELLENCAMP. Mark's MIDIed keyboard arpeggi in the second half of the second minute seem to relieve Steve R from his 12-string duties so he can pick up his electric axe. From here the song becomes just another from the day. Too bad. (8.75/10)8. "Hooks in You" (2:54) an opening that was lifted by Poland's COLLAGE for the fifth song of their 1991 album, Moonshine, "The Blues." It's too bad that I can't stop hearing that iconic song while listening to this one. Otherwise, it's a pretty good RICHARD MARX song. (8.75/10)9. "The Space..." (6:14) bouncy two-chord MIDI-ed synth strings keyboard chords slowly rise to the surface as the rest of the band and the two Steves join in, At 1:50 there is a switch into some heavier power chord to back Steve H during the chorus, but then we're back into the main motif of the verse for a bit before Steve H's rhythm guitar chord play leads the band into some more contemplative/reflective music and then, in the fifth minute, into a brief instrumental solo section. But then everything cuts out save for Mark's synth string washes and Steve H's 'distant' "everybody in the whole of the world" strainings. Cool section--cool vocal work (and music to support). And then it's done! (9/10)Total Time 50:35Hogarth trying to sound like Genesis, Paul Carrack (Ace, Mike + The Mechanics), or Paul Menel (IQ) doesn't work: he just becomes one of the many, but when Hogarth slows it down and brings in his sensitive approach he becomes something else: his own man, his own force, his own unique artist. � not included on vinyl LP releases (on CD only)B-/four stars; a solid NeoProg album that does beg for a little more sophistication and a little more maturity in the compositional department.

Featuring members of prog heavyweights Dream Theater, Spock's Beard, Marillion and The Flower Kings, this album comes out just one year after the release of their debut, and despite all still maintaining positions in the own respective, fulltime bands, there is a very palpable and effortless chemistry between everyone involved. With four songs totalling at a
items.body: Review by martindavey87 — Released in 2001, 'Bridge Across Forever' is the second album by progressive rock supergroup Transatlantic. Featuring members of prog heavyweights Dream Theater, Spock's Beard, Marillion and The Flower Kings, this album comes out just one year after the release of their debut, and despite all still maintaining positions in the own respective, fulltime bands, there is a very palpable and effortless chemistry between everyone involved. With four songs totalling at almost one hour and 20 minutes of music, this is an ambitious project, and will indeed take multiple listens to familiarise yourself with it all. There are so many twists and turns, every track is a journey through various musical ideas and themes, that it's just a matter of putting in the time. As you'd expect with musicians of this calibre, the performances and writing are of a high standard, and all four men doubling up on vocal duties keeps the songs sounding fresh and interesting. With particular highlights including tracks such as 'Duel With the Devil' and 'Stranger in Your Soul', 'Bridge Across Forever' is a worthy addition to any prog collection, and firmly establishes Transatlantic as more than just another side-project.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — The band's fourth studio album, second with singer Paul Menel at the microphone--plus they have the enlistment of Noel McCalla (Smallcreep's Day, Acting Very Strange), which excites me. All the names (except Paul's) are familiar to me. A February 1989 release, let's see what they've got for us!1. "War Heroes" (6:26) so what's wrong with Paul Menel's voice!? He sounds like any/every IQ singer--and he's definitely not bad. He holds pitch, he displays an appropriate level of emotional engagement with the lyrics and music. (8.875/10) 2. "Drive On" (4:57) like one of the "B" songs from a 1980s Genesis (or Phil Collins) song, very typical of music in the 1980s. Not bad, just . . . familiar. (8.75/10)3. "Nostalgia" (2:22) the instrumental intro to "Falling Apart ?" is quite Steve Hackett-ish--even down to the basic alternating-two-chord construction. Nice guitar work. Classic NeoProg/Genesis/Hackett bombast. (4.875/5)4. "Falling Apart at the Seams" (7:47) theatric and quite proficient. What are the criticisms of this band and album? This is as high quality NeoProg as I've ever heard (though I am by no means a fan or flaming advocate of the sub-genre). In the context of everything/anything I've ever heard from this band, this stands up there with any/all of it; if you're Genesis/NeoProg fan you've got to love this! Mike Holmes' guitar work and the overall sound palette and mix are quite extraordinary! (13.667/15)5. "Sold On You" (4:40) another typical 1980s offering that sounds like it came from Genesis or Mike + The Mechanics' "All I Need Is a Miracle" only with slightly proggier (and better) instrumental performances. The lyrics are just as cheesy as anything from the era. (8.875/10) 6. "Through My Fingers" (5:30) yes, that's Tony Banks taking on the BLUE NILE sound and style, only, like everybody else on the planet who loves and admires the band, they are unable to slow it down and strip it down to the degree that the Scots do. And we have yet another very solid performance from Paul Menel. (8.875/10)7. "Wurensh" (9:37) a prog-oriented band's obligatory "epic," this one plays out like a 1980s Genesis tune. I mean: exactly! Even the guitar arpeggi and syncopated bass and drum rhythm play is straight out of a Phil-Tony-Mike jam attempt. Granted, this is Paul Menel's weakest vocal performance on the album--partly do to the way his voice is mixed back into the soundscape, partly due to the fact that the band really didn't give him much to bite into. Great guitar work from Mike Holmes in the fifth minute. Plus, it is quite obvious that the band wanted this one to kick into symphonic-Yes-like territory--and they almost do; they just forgot to include/account for the importance of the lyrics, message, and vocal performance. Despite the flaws, I find it interesting to hear so much of Dutch NeoProg band KNIGHT AREA's Under a New Sign in this. Like my disappointment in Wobbler upon finding that their magnificent sound and melodies on 2011's Rites at Dawn had come from (almost directly lifted from) both Yes (Close to the Edge) and Gentle Giant's debut album. (17.5/20)8. "Nothing At All" (4:46) a solid representation of a pop-friendly prog song coming from a prog or even "classic rock" hair band of this era. Nothing to complain or get angry about as it is simply a purely-perfect represent of the popular music of the day. Fine performances all, plodding along as they all did at that time, with the same sound palette and pristine sound engineering of the day that everyone switching into the digital world were producing. (8.75/10) Total Time: 50:52Despite my love of Genesis' two 1976 studio albums (from which all things "NeoProg" came), I really don't know this band very well: though I've listened to pretty much every album they've ever made, I've never really felt "won over" by their achievements. Their sound palette doesn't repel me: it's rather warm and comforting; their vocalists or musicians and soloists always seem proficient and competent, their compositions aren't poor or repulsive. I think they're just . . . okay--very much like a 1980s Genesis song/album: Nice to listen to but nothing that will bring me back--nothing that wow's me as "That's new!" or "That's fresh!" Are You Sitting Comfortably represents, for me, a perfectly fitting and high-quality Genesis-like pop-friendly NeoProg of its day; nothing more and nothing less.B/four stars; a very solid, highly-respectable NeoProg album.

The tracks are exceedingly melodic, quintessentially adventurous in that they combine ornate passion with gritty exaltation and raised m
items.body: Review by tszirmay — This one came out of the blue, thanks to the ever present and hyper-active PROG ROGUE Research and Reconnaissance Department's irascible determination to seek out new nuggets of proggy bliss. The Freiburg based band has some seasoned musicians who have a communicative style, maximizing on emotional delivery and instrumental dexterity. The tracks are exceedingly melodic, quintessentially adventurous in that they combine ornate passion with gritty exaltation and raised my tired eyebrows more than once, and on each track! I went through this once while driving for work and I caught myself stopping a few times to marvel at my good fortune.The opener "Way to Cydonia" initially does open on a martial pulse, serving to assert the musical qualities of the players, what with the crunchy guitars and riffling keys but the mood immediately changes when the perfidious bass and smacking drums set the stage for the convincing vocal line, piano in tow as the arrangement expands in scope and sinks deep into the mind. The soft middle section is achingly beautiful , the piano and voice (lead and harmony) elevating to the choral melee with the tortuous lead guitar carving menacingly , as the rhythmic fury reaches a paroxysm. 'Sturm und Drang'!Now, here was the clincher! The next piece "Where is the Silence" was where I halted the first time on the autobahn, a delightfully melancholic, crushingly poignant tune that coalesces that stunning piano and elegant voice into an aural embrace verging on restrained perfection. A hymn for our times and a panacea for the soul. 'Ausgezeichnet'!The epic "Union of Souls" clocks in at 14 minutes + and falls into that classic progressive mold that elects to take its time in developing structure whilst telling an adventure. The initial section is measured in mellow despondence , until that moment where the atmosphere moves to a higher instrumental plain with a plaintive acoustic guitar phrasing at first, then a slowly expanding bass line, distant keyboard panting, marshaling drum beat and echoing pools of keys. When the volatile fury arrives, its purely orgasmic, a sizzling guitar streaks the sky, with mellotrons in tow. When singer Michael Bernauer clutches the microphone, his elegiac delivery veers from sullen to accepting. Majestic, powerful, lush and utterly moving. 'Wunderbar'!As proof of their professionalism, the band opts for two live tracks, which can be a risky move in some instances, but not here. On the contrary, the public display stamped this immediately with all the credentials need for a pentagon award. "Caravan of Slaves" begins with applause and military snare with thunderous percussives, as the caravan wanders into the sandstorm. Twirling synths and snake guitar lines serve up the Middle eastern theme perfectly, switching into a sweltering mini-jam session where each member is introduced on its instrument, the rotund bass guitar killing it as it rumbles over the dunes, aided by oasis guitars, palm tree keyboards and dromedary thumping drums. When they all coalesce into one musical pyramid, it's a pure joy to behold. I stopped again on the motorway as the word fun came to mind, or in German: 'Viel Spass'!The second live track "Already There" has a ghostly Floydian feel, with effect-laden voice in the hazy spotlight, a desperate whisper along with a doleful plea within a whopping melody and chorus that welds deep into the mind. Clanging guitar and Masonian beat keeps the mood reflective, spooky Wright keys and a fine electric guitar foray, right out of the Gilmourian manual. The harrowing vocal finale is simply devastating! 'Schon da'!I enjoyed this from the very first audition and subsequent revisits have only served to solidify my impressions! After all, both the Rogue and the Laz cannot be wrong at the same, that would be 'unm�glich' (Impossible). More, bitte!4.5 Martian Craters

But it was this album that made waves and set the standards for progressive rock music for the years to come. The first album that it wasn't bluesy at all, but instead it was heavy and dark. The opening track "21st century schizoid man" sounds exactly like what you would expect to hear by only looking the album cover. Someone could say it sounds almost like Heavy Metal. The frantic last part of the song leads to the next song "I talk to the wind", an ethereal prayer, where the band shows its' softer side. The first side of the record, closes with the timeless epic classic "Epitaph'. Simply one of the best songs ever written, generally in music. "Moonchild" opens the second side of the record and it's a spellbinding tune, with majestic sounds from Ian McDonald. The haunting last part of the song, with the distant sounds, it's the perfect prologue for the closing track of the album, "The court of the crimson king", a medieval-like epic. "In the court of the crimson king" is a cornerstone of progressive rock, and if you ask me, King Crimson never matched it. Glorious.

items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — The third album of my beloved Procol Harum, "A salty dog". The last one with Dave Knights on bass guitar and the last one as well with Matthew Fisher on keys, who he also did the production on this one. Now, "A salty dog", is a much more laid-back record than the two previous of the band, yet is so so beautiful. Mostly blues-based with a progressive direction, and always having the distinctive Procol Harum sound, meaning piano and voice driven. When Gary Brooker first performed the piece "A salty dog" on piano, the room was filled with sunlight shining through the windows. The drummer, B.J. Wilson, with a sunbeam on his face, told Brooker he thought it was the most beautiful song he had ever heard. Gary Brooker delivers some vein-cutting vocals throughout the album. Matthew Fisher did the lead vocals on three tracks on this one, "Boredom", "Wreck of the Hesperus" and "Pilgrim's progress". The track "Crucifiction" is a lament with ripping lead vocals provided by Robin Trower. A really beautiful album, closing a chapter for Procol Harum.

items.body: Review by UMUR — "For the Love of Art and the Making" is the third full-length studio album by Danish power/progressive metal act Beyond Twilight (if you discount the two Twilight albums as the works ofanother band). The album was released through Massacre Records in April 2006. It�s the successor to"Section X" from March 2005. There has been one lineup change since "Section X" as lead vocalistKelly Sundown Carpenter has been replaced by Swedish singer Bj�rn Jansson."For the Love of Art and the Making" is quite an interesting release as it�s basically one, 37:49minutes long composition broken down into 43 sub tracks. Stylistically it�s a continuation of thepower/progressive metal style of the preceding releases and as Jansson is a suitable and not toodifferent sounding replacement for Carpenter, the change on the lead vocalist spot doesn�t changemuch in terms of consistency of the band�s sound. The many short sub tracks makes "For the Love ofArt and the Making" a very different listening experience though as the tracks form only short partsof a longer track, they don�t have much time to evolve.It�s not that this is simple or one-dimensional music, because the tracks often shift in dynamicsbetween a heavy power/progressive metal oriented approach and more subtle and mellow parts. A normalverse/chorus structured composition wouldn�t work that way because it�s longer and you have time todevelop ideas over the course of a longer playing time. Here the short track lengths mean that ideasare executed fast and they flow by even faster. I�m not sure I think it always work that well,because sometimes I feel Beyond Twilight could have done a lot more with some of the parts, but atthat point they have usually already moved on to the next section. So, although "For the Love of Art and the Making" is a both well produced and well performedrelease, the songwriting approach will probably divide the waters. There�s arguably a lot of qualityhere but as an album I�m not sure I think "For the Love of Art and the Making" works that well. Tomy ears it�s more a study in interesting ideas and high level musicianship. Thinking of "For theLove of Art and the Making" as a single coherent composition doesn�t cross my mind while listeningto the album. The song is constantly disrupted and changes gears and dynamics and it�s actually abit stressful to listen to. When that is said "For the Love of Art and the Making" is still a highquality release, but I�m pretty sure it�s an acquired taste, so enter at your own risk. A 3.5 star(70%) rating is deserved.(Originally posted on Metal Music Archives).

items.body: Review by Abrasmatheus — Crime of the Century is an album that manages to balance the accessibility of pop rock with elements of greater musical complexity. Although it is often associated with Progressive Rock, I see it more as a progressive pop rock album, using progressive elements without fully committing to the more complex characteristics of the genre. This is especially evident in tracks such as "School" and "Rudy", which feature more elaborate structures and development.One of the album's greatest strengths is precisely this balance between melody and sophistication. The songs are quite accessible, but they never feel simplistic. There is clearly a lot of attention to arrangements, dynamics and development, allowing the album to work both as a collection of great melodies and as a record with plenty of interesting musical details.Among the tracks, "School" is one of the major highlights, with an excellent combination of atmosphere, instrumentation and development. "Hide in Your Shell" is also one of my favorites and, in particular, one of the tracks that best represents what I find special about this album. "Bloody Well Right" and "Asylum" are also excellent, while "Dreamer", despite being a very good song, takes a more direct and accessible approach.The instrumentation is another strong point. The saxophone is particularly distinctive and contributes greatly to the album's identity. The keyboards also play an important role, although I find the saxophone more impressive overall. The drums are very well played, while the guitar and bass are effective without necessarily being the instruments that stand out the most.But the biggest vocal highlight is undoubtedly Roger Hodgson. His voice has a very distinctive character and is immediately recognizable. His high register and particular way of delivering melodies give Supertramp an identity that I find difficult to compare with other bands. The vocal melodies are excellent and are probably among the strongest aspects of the entire album. Rick Davies also delivers very good vocals, but Hodgson's voice is more memorable to me.The production has aged extremely well. The mixing is excellent, and the instruments are very clearly defined, allowing each element to be heard without difficulty. The album has a very balanced sound and still works remarkably well decades after its release. A particularly interesting production moment is the final section of "Asylum", which creates a very engaging atmosphere.I also consider the themes of the album to be important. There is a predominantly melancholic atmosphere connected to the human and social issues addressed throughout the songs. Subjects such as education, isolation and other recurring social problems appear in different forms. The title Crime of the Century itself can be interpreted as a criticism of the problems created by society and the kind of prison that society can impose on individuals.The cover reinforces this idea very effectively. The image of what appears to be a prison fits the atmosphere of the album and can be interpreted as a symbolic representation of society and the limitations it imposes. It is a cover that I consider extremely appropriate for the album's content.Despite its qualities, I do not consider Crime of the Century one of the greatest examples of Progressive Rock in the strictest sense of the genre. Its historical importance is significant, but I believe there are many albums that are much more progressive and representative of the genre. For this reason, I would not necessarily recommend it as an introduction to Progressive Rock. It can work very well as a bridge between rock/pop and progressive music, but there are bands with much more complex approaches and much stronger connections to the genre.I also do not consider the album particularly innovative in terms of progressive music, although it contains some interesting ideas and has a very strong individual identity. In fact, one of the most difficult things about it is finding other bands to compare it with, since Supertramp has a very distinctive sound of its own.Among its strongest points are the very well-defined instrumentation, especially the saxophone and keyboards, Roger Hodgson's vocals, and the themes behind the songs. I do not see many significant weaknesses in the album. My main reservation concerns the final tracks: although they are good, I find the first part of the album stronger and more memorable. "Crime of the Century", the title track, is the song that impresses me the least, although I still consider it a good composition.Overall, I consider Crime of the Century a very good album, with an excellent balance between accessibility, strong melodies, sophisticated instrumentation, distinctive vocals and social themes. The opening tracks, especially "School" and "Hide in Your Shell", are among its greatest highlights, and the production remains impressive.It is not, for me, an essential Progressive Rock album in the strictest sense of the genre, but it is a high-quality record with a very strong identity. Its ability to naturally combine pop rock with progressive elements is precisely what makes it special.

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — The progressive metal movement, whose foundations were first laid in the mid-to-late 1980s by pioneers such as Queensr�che, Fates Warning, and Dream Theater, gained a much stronger identity and momentum during the 1990s, eventually expanding and establishing itself as a fully-fledged genre in the 2000s. Redemption belongs to the group of bands that emerged under that inspiring influence, shaping a powerful and virtuosic musical approach, immersed in the intricate structures of the most contemporary prog metal.With their self-titled 2003 debut album, Redemption had already shown what they were capable of, although it was still a somewhat raw and unpolished power-metal-style offering with nascent progressive elements. For "The Fullness of Time" (2005), their second album, the band led by Nick van Dyk brought in the duo James Sherwood (bass) and Chris Quirarte (drums), both from the ranks of the Los Angeles-based band Prymary, as their new rhythm section, and, most importantly, vocalist Ray Alder -who also fronted Fates Warning- evolving toward a more defined and mature sound.The first third of the album retains the band's seminal sound, with machine-gun-like, galloping riffs; frenzied, counterpointing solos between Bernie Versailles and van Dyk; and Quirarte's wild double-bass drumming, to which van Dyk's keyboards add an additional, fitting melodic and atmospheric layer, both on the aggressive "Threads," the fast-paced "Scarred," and the reflective and bitter "Parker's Eyes" -which offers a somber and disheartening view of the world, including a reference to the events of 9/11- and incorporates a beautiful, arpeggiated acoustic nuance before exploding instrumentally.The following two-thirds reflect the band's solidity and progressive character, with the epic "Sapphire", a powerful and expansive instrumental tapestry led by a spirited Alder on vocals and generous with guitar and synthesizer solos, contrasted with calm, refreshing passages -the jewel of the album- and the intricate "The Fullness of Time," a suite divided into four sections where journeys through rocky peaks -the furious and vengeful "i. Rage" and the resilient "iii. Release"- alternate with clear, evocative sonic valleys -the meditative "ii. Despair" and the hopeful and luminous "iv. Trascendence"."The Fullness of Time" marked a turning point in Redemption's career: an album in which the band left behind the rough edges of its debut to find its own identity, delivering one of the genre's strongest offerings of the mid-2000s.4/4.5 stars

items.body: Review by martindavey87 — Released in 2007 through the bands official fan club, 'Images and Words 15th Anniversary Performance' is literally what it says it is; Dream Theater playing the entire album that forever set the standard for all progressive metal bands to follow. Of course, it has its pros and cons. There's some interesting embellishments dotted around, which could keep us prog nerds at least somewhat invested for a little while, and it's cool to hear Jordan Rudess interpret some of Kevin Moore's keyboard parts. Then of course, there's vocalist James LaBrie. Sure, he struggles with some of it due to age and a well-documented vocal injury, but I guess at least he's trying. The band would go on to release a 25th anniversary performance of this album through their 'Lost Not Forgotten' series many years later, so, you know, it's probably slightly better than that one, again, due to LaBrie being another ten years older by then and struggling even more. Bless him. I don't think I'd ever choose to actually listen to this over the original 1992 studio album, which, for the record, is my favourite album of all time. But the name of this release describes exactly what you're getting here, so there's absolutely no point in taking it too seriously. It's a cool addition to the collection, and if you're a die-hard Dream Theater fan like I am, then you'll enjoy owning it. Simple as that.
